restyle_prompt: Edit the image into a centered portrait. Re-pose the subject into a natural, neutral, square-on posture, with the face and visible body oriented toward the camera. Animals and creatures face the camera sitting or standing naturally; only if the source shows them lying, curled, or turned away, re-pose them sitting or standing. Center the subject on the image's vertical midline: the head must be exactly horizontally centered, with equal white space to its left and right. Keep tails, wings, and held items close to the body so the head stays centered; never let a tail push the head off center. Do not preserve a side-facing or three-quarter body angle from the source. Preserve exact identity, facial features, distinctive details, and the exact colors of every part, including ears, markings, and patterns; never recolor any part. Preserve natural proportions; do not stretch, elongate, or squash the face, head, or rigid characters. Preserve the character's expression, the subject's mouth must be slightly open. Frame the subject with comfortable breathing room: the entire head, including ears, horns, antennae, hair, and the top of the head, must be fully visible, with a small white margin above it and on both sides. Choose the framing by body shape. Compact characters whose whole body is roughly as wide as it is tall, such as four-legged animals, sitting animals, round creatures, and characters whose head with ears already fills about 40% of the width at full body: if the source shows the full body, keep the whole body, including the feet and tail, inside the frame with clear white space on the top, both sides, and below it; never let the body or tail touch the left, right, or top edge; place the full body in the vertical middle of the frame, with about equal white space above the head and below the feet. People, gorillas, monkeys and other apes, and humanoid characters with realistic proportions, whose head is small compared with their body height: never show them full body, even when the source shows them crouching or on all fours; frame them from about the waist or hips up, placed high in the frame, so the head, including hair or hat, is about 55% of the image width and the body continues off the bottom edge of the frame. Cartoon characters with big heads, where the head is about a third of the total height or more, are shown full body standing, scaled so the head is at least 40% of the image width, with the legs and feet the source shows, placed in the vertical middle of the frame with about equal white space above and below. A single object or food character is shown whole, scaled up to fill most of the frame. In every other case, size the subject so the head, including ears and hair, is about 50% of the image width: never narrower than 40% and never wider than 60% of it. For characters whose ears, horns, or antennae are taller than the head itself, size the head without them and keep them fully in the frame above it. If the character has shoulders, keep both shoulders fully inside the frame. Only draw legs and feet that the source shows, matching them in number, shape, length, and design; never invent legs or feet the source does not show. A compact character shown with its feet keeps its full body with white space below if needed. Any other body that is cut off continues all the way to the bottom edge of the frame; never end the subject in a straight horizontal cut with white space below it. Never add arms, legs, hands, a torso, or any body part the source character does not have, and never lengthen or stretch the body; a character that is only a head or a blob stays that way. Do not add clothing, collars, tags, jewelry, accessories, or props that are not in the source. If the character is only a head or a single object, show the entire character with a small white margin around it. Photorealistic people and selfies need a wider framing than the source: zoom out to a portrait from the upper chest up, placed high in the frame, with the head, including hair, about 35-40% of the image width, the full hair, chin, neck, and both shoulders visible, a small white margin above the hair of about 5% of the image height, and the chest continuing to the bottom edge. Never add, remove, or change clothing: keep exactly what the source shows. For photorealistic people, create the extra room by adding white space above and beside the head and widening the existing shoulders; continue only the clothing already visible, and if the source shows bare shoulders, keep them as they are and let the body leave the bottom edge at the upper chest, never revealing more of the chest than the source. Maintain a pure white (#FFFFFF) background.
crop_prompt:
This is a portrait of a character. A SQUARE crop will be taken from it. The square is the FULL WIDTH of the image and moves only vertically.
Give the vertical CENTRE of the square for a video call.
The square MUST show the character's entire head, including the tips of ears, horns, antennae, hair, and anything that forms the top of the character such as a hat, cap, or mushroom top. The square does not need to show the feet or lower body. Leave headroom: the topmost point of the head should sit about 8-12% of the square's height below the top edge of the square, never touching it. Within that, keep the eyes and mouth as close to the vertical centre of the square as possible. Photorealistic people are the exception to the headroom rule: centre the midpoint between the eyes and the mouth in the square, and let the top of the hair be cut if needed. Tall ears exception: if the ears, horns, or antennae rising above the skull are taller than the head itself (skull top to chin), do not fit their full length; show the skull top plus at most two thirds of a head-height of them, let their tips be cut, and keep the face near the middle of the square. If hair or the head itself is too tall to fit with headroom, place the square as high as possible while keeping the chin inside. A hat, cap, or mushroom top is not an ear: always keep it fully inside the square with a small margin above it. In every case keep the entire face from the eyebrows down to the chin visible, with a small margin below the chin.
Output ONLY JSON and nothing else. All position values are fractions of the image HEIGHT (0 = top, 1 = bottom); confidence is 0 to 1.
Example output:
{"crop_y":0.5,"eyes_y":0.5,"mouth_y":0.5,"head_top_y":0.5,"skull_top_y":0.5,"chin_y":0.5,"photorealistic_person":false,"confidence":0.5}
crop_y is the centre of the square and is the value used for framing. eyes_y, mouth_y, head_top_y and chin_y are the vertical positions of the eyes, the mouth, the topmost point of the head (ear/horn/antenna/hair tips), and the chin. skull_top_y is the top of the head not counting ears, horns, or antennae; a hat, cap, helmet, or mushroom top counts as part of the head. The chin is the bottom of the face just below the mouth, never the bottom of a body or object that has a face on it. photorealistic_person is true only for a photograph or photorealistic image of a real human. confidence is how confident you are in crop_y. Only crop_y is required; still provide the others as your best estimate.
